questions.prompt: How does Andreyev characterize “music theory” relative to a scientific theorem?
choices: A As identical to a scientific theorem that predicts new laws of sound.
B As a body of past practices that persist into the present, not a scientific theorem.
C As a set of mandatory creative rules every composer must invent anew.
D As exclusively electronic-music programming techniques.
questions.explain: He stresses music theory is an unusual term because it is not like a scientific theorem; it is a body of past practices.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, music theory knowledge is primarily:
choices: A Prescriptive—telling you exactly what you must compose.
B Descriptive—showing what has been done (grammar/syntax of the tradition).
C Limited to marketing popular songs.
D Only useful for non-Western improvisation and never for notation.
questions.explain: He insists it is descriptive, not prescriptive: it teaches grammar and syntax so musicians can communicate.

questions.prompt: Which two features does Andreyev highlight as especially distinguishing the Western musical tradition?
choices: A Oral-only transmission and exclusive monophony.
B Writing music down (notation) and an emphasis on polyphony.
C Ban on clefs and avoidance of rhythm.
D Mandatory electronic synthesis and no staff notation.
questions.explain: He pairs a largely written tradition (notation) with Western emphasis on polyphony (also noted at 1.12).

questions.prompt: On the ruled staff, how does vertical position map onto pitch?
choices: A Higher on the staff means lower pitch; lower means higher pitch.
B Lower on the staff is lower sound; higher on the staff is higher sound (spatial metaphor).
C Staff height only encodes loudness, never pitch.
D Pitch is encoded only by ink color, not position.
questions.explain: The staff uses a spatial metaphor: bottom = lower sound, top = higher sound.

questions.prompt: In North American nomenclature, what note names correspond to the spaces of the treble staff (bottom to top), per Andreyev’s mnemonic?
choices: A E-G-B-D-F
B F-A-C-E (“FACE”)
C G-B-D-F-A
D A-C-E-G
questions.explain: He recalls the childhood mnemonic F-A-C-E for the spaces; lines are E-G-B-D-F (1.46).
